title: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)
summary: Chest compressions and rescue breaths for someone in sudden cardiac or respiratory arrest.
steps: 1. Make sure the scene is safe for you and the person.
2. Shake their shoulder and ask loudly, "Are you all right?"
3. If there is no response, point to a specific person: "You in the blue shirt, call 115 now and find an AED if there is one."
4. Lay the person on their back on a firm, flat surface.
5. Place the heel of one hand in the center of the chest (lower half of the breastbone) and lace your other hand on top.
6. Keep your elbows straight and use your upper-body weight to press straight down 5–6 cm.
7. COMPRESS AT 100–120 TIMES PER MINUTE. Count out loud: 1, 2, 3... 30.
8. If you are trained, give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions. If you are not, keep doing continuous chest compressions (hands-only CPR).
cautions: Do NOT pause compressions for more than 10 seconds between cycles.
Do NOT bend your elbows while compressing. That weakens each push.
Let the chest recoil fully after every compression.

title: Stopping bleeding from an open wound
summary: Control external bleeding and reduce the risk of life-threatening blood-loss shock.
steps: 1. Wear medical gloves or a clean plastic bag to protect yourself from blood-borne infection.
2. Press sterile gauze or a clean cloth directly on the bleeding wound.
3. Push hard and continuously for at least 10–15 minutes without letting go.
4. Wrap a roller bandage tightly over the gauze to hold it in place.
5. If blood soaks through, add a new layer on top and keep wrapping. Do NOT peel off the first layer.
6. Raise the injured limb above the heart if there is no fracture.
7. If a major limb artery is severed (bright red blood spurting) and pressure fails, place a tourniquet about 5 cm above the wound, write down the time, and loosen it for 1–2 minutes once an hour.
cautions: Do NOT put tobacco powder, animal hair, mud, or unknown herbs on an open wound.
Do NOT pull out a large embedded object (knife, metal, or wood). It may be plugging the bleeding.

title: First aid for thermal burns
summary: Cool the burned skin at once to lower the temperature and limit deeper tissue damage.
steps: 1. Move the person away from the heat, or put out burning clothes by having them stop, drop, and roll.
2. SOAK OR RUN COOL CLEAN WATER (15–20°C) over the burn continuously for 15–20 minutes.
3. Gently remove jewelry, watches, and tight clothing from the burned area BEFORE it swells.
4. Cover the burn loosely with clean sterile gauze or clean plastic wrap.
5. Have them sip warm water with a little salt, or an oral rehydration solution.
6. Go to a clinic if the burn is larger than the palm, or if it is on the face, eyes, a joint, or the genitals.
cautions: Do NOT put ice or an ice pack directly on the burn. That can cause frostbite and tissue death.
Do NOT apply toothpaste, fish sauce, python fat, or egg yolk to a burn.
Do NOT break blisters. The raised skin is a natural sterile cover.

title: Splinting a fracture
summary: Immobilize the joint above and below the break to reduce pain and the risk of traumatic shock.
steps: 1. Do not move the person until the suspected fracture is splinted, unless the scene is extremely dangerous.
2. Use a wooden board, a straight stick, or stiff cardboard longer than the broken section.
3. The splint must be long enough to IMMOBILIZE BOTH JOINTS: one above and one below the break.
4. Pad the bone ends and every place the splint touches skin with cloth or soft cotton.
5. Tie the splint above and below the break. Do not tie directly over the fracture.
6. Check circulation: feel a pulse, or check that fingers or toes stay warm and pink after the splint is tied.
cautions: Do NOT try to realign or straighten a bone that is out of line.
If it is an open fracture (bone through the skin), do NOT push the bone back in. Cover the area with a clean dressing.

title: Choking (Heimlich maneuver)
summary: Create pressure that pushes a blocked airway clear and keeps the person from suffocating.
steps: 1. Recognize it: they suddenly clutch their throat, cannot speak or cough out loud, and their face turns blue.
2. Stand behind them and wrap both arms around their waist.
3. Make a fist and place the thumb side on the upper abdomen, just above the navel and below the breastbone.
4. Grasp that fist with your other hand.
5. THRUST HARD AND FAST INWARD AND UPWARD to drive air behind the object.
6. Repeat up to 5 times. Alternate with back blows between the shoulder blades if needed.
7. If they become unconscious, lay them on their back and start CPR at once.
cautions: Do NOT sweep a finger blindly into the throat if you cannot see the object. You can push it deeper.
For an infant under 1 year, use 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts. Do NOT use the adult Heimlich maneuver.

title: Heat exhaustion and heatstroke
summary: Cool the body urgently when it can no longer regulate temperature and fever rises above 40°C.
steps: 1. Move the person at once into shade, a breeze, or a cool air-conditioned room.
2. Undo shirt buttons and loosen belts and tight clothing.
3. Cool the whole body: spray cool water, wipe the skin with a wet cloth, and fan them.
4. Place cool packs or wet cloths on LARGE BLOOD-VESSEL AREAS: armpits, groin, and both sides of the neck.
5. If they are fully awake, give small sips of cool water or oral rehydration solution.
6. Go to a hospital at once if they are drowsy, seizing, or vomiting.
cautions: Do NOT give paracetamol or aspirin. They do not treat heatstroke and can harm the liver or kidneys.
Do NOT give water to someone who is unconscious or drowsy. They can inhale it into the lungs.
